headline: Bond Selloff Deepens as Fed Hike Nears; PPI Tame
tileReason: The daily 30-year average jumped to 7.42% Thursday as a weak 30-year bond sale and Fed hike talk pushed the 10-year yield above 5.1%; this morning's milder wholesale inflation report hasn't brought yields down yet.
takeaway:
Rates climbed again Thursday. The daily 30-year average rose to 7.42% from 7.30%, its second straight jump of 0.12% and the highest since early October. Freddie Mac's weekly survey showed 7.11%, but that number mostly reflects quotes gathered before this week's selloff, so it lags what borrowers are seeing now.

A weak bond sale added to the pressure. The Treasury's $25 billion sale of 30-year bonds Thursday afternoon drew soft demand for the second day in a row, and it had to pay a slightly higher yield than the market expected to sell it all. The 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, finished Thursday around 5.10% to 5.13% depending on the source, up from about 4.98% Tuesday.

Fed officials kept the hike talk going. Several officials who spoke Thursday, including Cleveland's Beth Hammack and Philadelphia's Anna Paulson, said more gradual increases look appropriate, while Vice Chair Michelle Bowman sounded more cautious about the cost to rate-sensitive parts of the economy like housing. After this morning's data, futures markets put the odds of a quarter-point hike on Dec 9 at roughly 85% to 91%, with the rest on a bigger half-point move, so some kind of hike is close to fully expected.

This morning's wholesale inflation report was a little milder than feared. Producer prices, what businesses charge each other, rose 0.3% in October versus 0.4% expected, after September's 1.3% surge; prices excluding food and energy rose 0.3%, as expected. Yields dipped briefly on the news, then the 10-year drifted back to about 5.15%, so it hasn't given borrowers relief so far.

Lenders still have some cushion. The Optimal Blue conforming index, which tracks rates on loans borrowers actually locked, sat about 2.17% above the 10-year Treasury on Nov 9, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That extra room means lenders don't have to pass along every bit of a bond-market selloff, which helps explain why mortgage rates have risen less than Treasury yields over the past month.

Next week brings more tests. October retail sales and Nvidia's earnings come Tuesday, the minutes of the Fed's October meeting come Wednesday, then the Fed's preferred inflation measure on Nov 25, the Dec 4 jobs report and the Dec 9 Fed decision.

fedOdds.title: Odds of a Fed hike on Dec 9
fedOdds.source: CME FedWatch via FXEmpire (Nov 13); money-market pricing via TokenPost (9:08 AM ET Nov 13); Trading Economics (Nov 13); Thursday reading from Options Oracle and Trading Economics (Nov 12)
fedOdds.note: Sources differ on how they count. CME FedWatch via FXEmpire shows about 90% for a quarter-point hike and 10% for a half point (down from about 14% before the PPI report), so a hike of some size is near 100%. TokenPost reports 91% / 9%, and Trading Economics cites about 85% for a quarter point.

drivers.title: Weak demand at the 30-year bond sale
drivers.text: Thursday's $25 billion 30-year bond sale had to pay a slightly higher yield than expected and drew the weakest demand since June, following a soft 10-year sale Tuesday. When investors need extra yield to absorb all that new government debt, long-term yields rise, and mortgage rates went up 0.12% Thursday.

drivers.title: Fed officials keep a December hike on track
drivers.text: Most Fed officials speaking this week, including Hammack and Paulson, said further gradual increases look appropriate, and Goolsbee said inflation looks to be going the wrong way. With a Dec 9 hike close to fully expected and more possible early next year, longer-term yields and mortgage rates have a hard time falling.

drivers.title: Inflation still running hot
drivers.text: Tuesday's consumer price report came in above forecasts, and this morning's wholesale prices are up 6.5% from a year ago, the most since 2022. Even though October's monthly wholesale rise was a bit below forecasts, persistent inflation keeps bond investors demanding higher yields.

drivers.title: Milder-than-feared wholesale prices
drivers.text: Producer prices rose 0.3% in October versus 0.4% expected, and the odds of a bigger half-point Fed move slipped from about 14% to about 10%. That briefly pulled yields lower this morning, though the 10-year has since moved back up to about 5.15%.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates still far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The Optimal Blue conforming index sat about 2.17% above the 10-year Treasury yield on Nov 9, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That wide gap is a cushion: lenders can absorb part of a jump in Treasury yields without raising rates as much.

outlook.baseSource: Mortgage News Daily, Nov 12 close (latest available)
outlook.basis: The odds still lean a bit toward higher rates, but less than Thursday, because 7.42% already prices in much of this week's selloff. Working against borrowers: the 10-year Treasury yield is around 5.15%, demand at this week's 10-year and 30-year bond sales was weak, and a December Fed hike is close to fully expected. In borrowers' favor: this morning's wholesale inflation report was milder than feared, mortgage rates still sit unusually far above the 10-year Treasury (about 2.17% vs. a long-run average near 1.76%), and housing data are softening. Big swing events: Tuesday's retail sales, the Nov 25 report on the Fed's preferred inflation measure, the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision and oil headlines tied to Iran.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: The daily 30-year average reached 7.42% Thursday after two quick jumps this week, its highest since early October, though still below the 7.6%-plus levels of early last month. This morning's milder wholesale inflation report hasn't pulled bond yields down yet. If you're under contract or close to it, talk with Stuart about how locking, a float-down option (which lets you take a lower rate if rates drop after you lock), or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates turned higher this week after a month of easing, and October home sales fell 5.5%, so buyers are feeling the pinch. With a December Fed hike widely expected, realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to lower their rate, can help a home stand out.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates jumped to about 7.42% this week as bond yields climbed above 5.1% on hot inflation, weak bond sales and a widely expected December Fed hike.
